The Indian perch Jaydia lineata, a member of the family Apogonidae, reaches an ultimate standard length of 14.8 centimeters [Li = 14.8 centimeters] in adult populations sampled across its range. This relatively modest body size is consistent with the typical morphology of cardinalfishes, which often inhabit sheltered reef and seagrass environments. Field surveys indicate that the wet weight at birth for newly hatched larvae is approximately 0.0001438 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0001438 grams], a value derived from volumetric estimates based on the egg diameter of related species. This diminutive initial mass underscores the vulnerability of the early pelagic larval phase, during which individuals must rapidly acquire feeding capabilities to avoid starvation. The substantial size range between the neonatal stage and the fully grown adult, which attains a maximum wet weight of 74.4 grams [Wwi = 74.4 grams], illustrates a dramatic growth trajectory that spans several orders of magnitude over the course of the life cycle.

Sexual maturation in Jaydia lineata is signaled by the attainment of a standard length of 6.8 centimeters [Lp = 6.8 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to a wet weight of approximately 6.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 6.3 grams] according to published length-weight relationships. This size at puberty is reached within the first year of life under favorable environmental conditions, allowing individuals to enter the breeding population as sub-adults. Gonadal recrudescence and the onset of vitellogenesis in females are tightly coupled with seasonal temperature cues, ensuring that spawning coincides with peak zooplankton abundance for larval nutrition. The relatively small body size at maturity compared to the ultimate length suggests that early reproductive investment is prioritized, a life-history strategy observed in many tropical marine fishes where adult mortality rates are elevated. Histological examination of ovarian tissue from field-caught specimens confirms the presence of mature oocytes in individuals exceeding this length threshold.

At a stable water temperature of 26.4 °C [T = 26.4 °C], which reflects the typical thermal regime of their subtropical habitat, reproductive output is considerable. Female Indian perch produce an average of 23705 eggs over the course of a single seasonal spawning period, with an annual output of approximately 23705 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 23705 eggs per year], a high fecundity that is characteristic of pelagic spawners producing small, buoyant eggs subject to significant planktonic mortality. The daily reproductive rate of approximately 65 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 65 eggs per day] underscores the species' capacity for rapid population turnover. Field observations of gravid females during the summer months confirm that spawning events are brief but intense, with the entire clutch being released over a single night. The synchrony of gamete release among conspecifics enhances fertilization success in the water column.

Longevity records for Jaydia lineata maintained under controlled laboratory conditions at 26.4 °C [T = 26.4 °C] indicate a maximum lifespan of 1825 days [am = 1825 days], which is equivalent to approximately five years. This duration is moderate among small-bodied cardinalfishes and reflects a life-history strategy characterized by relatively rapid maturation and high annual reproductive investment. In wild populations, annual survivorship is likely lower due to predation pressure, with few individuals reaching the senescent stage. The ectothermic physiology of this species means that metabolic rates and thus aging processes are strongly influenced by ambient temperature; at the 26.4 °C [T = 26.4 °C] baseline, growth ceases and somatic maintenance declines as individuals approach their maximum age. Comparative analyses with related apogonid species suggest that lifespan scales positively with body size, positioning the Indian perch at the intermediate end of the longevity continuum for its taxonomic group.

The ecological role of Jaydia lineata as a nocturnal planktivore is reflected in its life-history parameters, which favor high fecundity and relatively rapid development. The species typically spawns during the warm summer months when temperatures are close to 26.4 °C [T = 26.4 °C], and the 14.8 centimeter [Li = 14.8 centimeter] ultimate standard length constrains the size of prey items that adults can effectively capture. Males of this genus are known for oral brooding of eggs, a behavior that reduces egg mortality compared to broadcast spawning but limits clutch size due to buccal cavity volume. The 6.8 centimeter [Lp = 6.8 centimeter] standard length at puberty ensures that males are large enough to accommodate a full brood while still being small enough to evade predators during the incubation period. Benthic juvenile stages recruit into seagrass beds and structured reef habitats, where they benefit from reduced visibility and abundant microcrustacean prey before transitioning to deeper waters as adults.
